prime.problem: Stacking more blocks and widening them makes the numbers flowing through the network drift in size from layer to layer, and a 10.8M-parameter model on 1M characters starts memorising the training text instead of learning Shakespeare.
prime.fits: The residual card gave the block a clean x + f(x) path and reached val 2.08. This card adds the two stabilisers that let Karpathy scale that block up: LayerNorm (BatchNorm from the makemore course, turned to work per token) and dropout.
expect: LayerNorm: normalise each token's features, not each feature across the batch
dropout: zero 20%, scale the rest by 1.25
the scaled-up gpt.py config and its 10,788,929 parameters
prime.goal: Explain why LayerNorm replaces BatchNorm in a Transformer, where the norms and dropouts sit in a pre-norm block, and count gpt.py's parameters yourself; then decide how to train it on your own laptop.

attend: Which one-character change turns Karpathy's BatchNorm1d into a LayerNorm, and why does it remove the need for running averages?
Why does the block normalise the input to each sublayer rather than the residual stream itself?
Why are dropout's survivors multiplied by 1.25, and what would break at test time if they weren't?
Which of gpt.py's knobs add most of the 10.79M parameters, and which barely add any?
Why does the lecture only switch dropout on at the moment the model gets big?

must: LayerNorm takes the mean and variance over one token's C features (dim 1), not over the batch (dim 0) → each token's output depends only on itself → no running averages, identical behaviour in training and at batch-1 generation → it fits a Transformer where BatchNorm doesn't

Pre-norm puts LayerNorm inside the branch, x + sa(ln1(x)) → the residual stream itself is never normalised → gradients still have a plain addition path from the loss back to the embeddings → deeper stacks keep training; post-norm puts a norm on that path in every block

Dropout zeroes a random 20% each step and scales the rest by 1/0.8 = 1.25 → the expected value of every activation is unchanged → the net can't rely on any single unit and trains an ensemble of thinned sub-networks → less memorisation; in eval() it is switched off with nothing to rescale

Scaling C from 32 to 384 → parameters grow roughly with n_layer × C² (12 × 6 × 384² ≈ 10.6M of the 10.79M) → a model with about 10.7 parameters per training character → val drops to 1.48 only because dropout 0.2 holds back the overfitting
elevated: Karpathy's hand-written x.var divides by C − 1 while nn.LayerNorm divides by C → outputs differ slightly (max 0.0161 at C = 100) → matching the two in a test needs unbiased=False
gpt.py on MPS measured 1.27 s per training step → 5,000 steps ≈ 1.8 h plus ≈ 30 min of evals → the Colab's 209,729-parameter config (1.83 in 158 s on CPU) is the practical laptop run
reference: nn.Dropout(dropout) at three places: attention weights after softmax, after the multi-head proj, end of FeedFoward
gpt.py hyperparameters: batch 64, block 256, n_embd 384, 6 heads, 6 layers, dropout 0.2, lr 3e-4, 5000 iters
the Colab's small config: n_embd 64, 4 heads, 4 layers, block 32, batch 16, lr 1e-3, dropout 0

compress.prompt: Without scrolling up, draw one pre-norm Block as a flow from x to the next x, marking every LayerNorm and every dropout. Then say in 3–4 sentences why LayerNorm and not BatchNorm, and why dropout arrives only when the model is scaled up.
checklist: LayerNorm normalises each token's C features on its own; BatchNorm normalises each feature across the batch
no batch dependence, so no running stats and the same behaviour in training and generation
pre-norm: ln1 before sa, ln2 before ffwd, ln_f before lm_head; the residual stream is only ever added to
dropout after the softmax, after proj, and at the end of ffwd; off in eval()
survivors scaled by 1/(1 − p) = 1.25 so the expected value is unchanged
10.79M parameters on ~1M training characters would overfit, so dropout 0.2 comes in with the scale-up

retrieve.q: Explain what LayerNorm guarantees about the vector each sublayer receives, and why that is useful when blocks are stacked six deep.
answer: every token vector enters sa and ffwd with mean 0 and std 1 across its features (before γ, β)
so the input scale no longer depends on how much earlier blocks have added to the stream
γ and β let the net learn a different scale where that helps

retrieve.q: Walk through what one nn.Dropout(0.2) does to a vector of ten 1s in training mode and then after model.eval().
answer: training: each entry is zeroed with probability 0.2, the rest become 1/0.8 = 1.25 (the lab got two zeros)
the expected value stays 0.8 × 1.25 = 1.0
a fresh mask is drawn on every forward pass
eval: the vector passes through unchanged, all 1.0

retrieve.q: Trace where LayerNorm is applied in a (B, T, C) tensor: which numbers share one mean and variance?
answer: the C = 384 features of one token at one position in one sequence
B and T both act as batch dimensions: B × T separate normalisations
no statistics are shared across tokens or sequences

retrieve.q: You have one evening on the M3. Choose between running gpt.py in full, --gpt --quick, and --colab. What does each cost and what does each show you?
answer: full gpt.py: about 2¼ h (1.27 s/step × 5,000 plus ~30 min of evals); should approach the video's 1.48
--gpt --quick: 533 s for 250 steps, val 2.39: shows the loss falling and the speed, not the result
--colab: 158 s on CPU to val 1.83 with 209,729 params: the full training curve of a real (small) Transformer

compare.q: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm: they share the formula, so what is fundamentally different, which choice of axis causes it, and when would you still pick BatchNorm?
answer: BatchNorm: statistics per feature across the batch; LayerNorm: per example across its features
the axis choice makes BatchNorm couple examples and need running mean/var for test time; LayerNorm needs neither
BatchNorm still suits conv nets on images with large, stable batches
BatchNorm fails at batch size 1 and with variable-length sequences; LayerNorm can't use cross-example statistics at all

compare.q: Residual connections and pre-norm LayerNorm both address "deep stacks train badly". Which part of the problem does each solve, and what would each alone fail at?
answer: residual: gives gradients a plain addition path, so depth doesn't strangle them (3 blocks without it: 2.33; with it, plus projections and a 4× FFN: 2.08)
pre-norm LayerNorm: keeps each sublayer's input at a steady scale as the stream grows
residual alone lets the stream's size drift; LayerNorm alone (without the skip) still leaves a long multiplicative chain
pre-norm is designed to sit on top of the residual path without breaking it

predict.q: Before training, γ = 1 and β = 0 in ln_f. For gpt.py (C = 384), every token vector leaving ln_f has the same length, whatever came in. Commit to a number for that length (its L2 norm, the square root of the sum of squares).
predict.answer: About √384 ≈ 19.60. After normalising, the 384 numbers have mean 0 and variance 1 (dividing by C), so their squares sum to 384. On 1,000 random rows with mean 5 and std 3, nn.LayerNorm(384) gives an average norm of 19.5959. LayerNorm doesn't only centre a vector. It puts every token on the same sphere, so lm_head sees inputs of a fixed size until γ learns otherwise.

apply.task: With pencil and paper, count the parameters of the Colab's small config (n_embd 64, 4 heads, 4 layers, block 32, vocab 65) the way the card counts gpt.py: q/k/v, proj, the two ffwd layers and the two LayerNorms per Block, then the token and position tables, ln_f and lm_head. Then predict how many parameters doubling block_size to 64 would add.
apply.done: You get 49,792 per Block, 199,168 for 4 Blocks, plus 4,160 + 2,048 + 128 + 4,225 = 209,729 (what the lab prints), and doubling block_size adds only 32 × 64 = 2,048 (one bigger position table).
apply.hint: Each Linear has in × out weights plus out biases, except q, k and v, which have no bias. Each LayerNorm has 2 × 64.
